props.title: Guess Who

sections.content: Guess Who (2005) flips the racial dynamics of the groundbreaking Guess Who's Coming to Dinner (1967), transforming Stanley Kramer's serious examination of interracial relationships into a mainstream comedy. Ashton Kutcher steps into the Sidney Poitier role as the white boyfriend meeting his Black girlfriend's family, with Bernie Mac taking the Spencer Tracy patriarch position. While lighter in tone than its predecessor, the film tackles persistent social anxieties about interracial relationships through humor, using comedy to disarm audiences while still addressing prejudice and family acceptance.

sections.content: The evolution of interracial relationship portrayals in American cinema reflects shifting social attitudes. Jungle Fever (1991) took an unflinching look at the complexities and prejudices surrounding Black-white relationships, while Monster's Ball (2001) earned Halle Berry an Oscar for her portrayal of a relationship complicated by racial tension and tragedy. More recent films like The Big Sick (2017) have expanded the conversation beyond the Black-white binary to explore cross-cultural relationships in all their complexity.

Comedy has proven particularly effective at addressing racial dynamics, with films like Get Out (2017) using genre elements to examine racial anxiety in interracial relationships. Away We Go (2009) and Loving (2016) took more grounded approaches, examining how mixed couples navigate family expectations and societal pressure. These films demonstrate how far American cinema has come since anti-miscegenation laws influenced early Hollywood's portrayal of relationships. SUBHEAD: Modern Takes on Cross-Cultural Romance

sections.content: Contemporary films increasingly treat interracial relationships as incidental rather than central plot points. To All the Boys I've Loved Before (2018) features a mixed-race protagonist without making her identity the focus of the story. Similarly, Everything, Everything (2017) and The Sun Is Also a Star (2019) incorporate cultural differences into broader coming-of-age narratives, suggesting a gradual normalization of interracial relationships in mainstream cinema.
